relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: An adversarial force incites David to convert people into a royal number.
The census runs from border to border so the king may know his military possession.
Joab objects that the people already belong to themselves and to Divine care, not to David's need for control.
Royal command overrules ethical resistance.
More than a million bodies become sword-drawing statistics.
Joab leaves two tribes uncounted because the order remains abhorrent.
The royal act is judged, but the people are struck.
David confesses after the machinery has already moved.
A word comes through Gad the seer.
The king is offered three collective catastrophes as his choice.
Gad places the terrible options before him.
Famine, war, and plague all make ordinary bodies pay for royal failure.
David chooses what he calls the merciful hand, though others will bear it.
Seventy thousand people die.
At Jerusalem the destroying hand is finally told: Enough—release.
The sword over the city drives king and elders to the ground.
David at last asks why the people suffer for his command.
The next step leads toward Ornan's threshing floor.
David follows Gad's instruction.
Ornan's four sons hide while their father continues threshing wheat beneath terror.
A Jebusite landowner bows as the king approaches during plague.
David requests the land for an altar and ties the transaction to stopping death.
Ornan offers land, animals, tools, and grain under a power imbalance the text cannot make disappear.
David insists on paying rather than making another person's loss his sacrifice.
The Chronicler records a vast gold price for the site.
An altar, offerings, prayer, and fire mark the end of the plague sequence.
The sword returns to its sheath.
David begins worship at the Jebusite threshing floor.
The older sanctuary remains at Gibeon.
David's fear of the sword prevents him from approaching it.

contemplative_note: A ruler counts; seventy thousand die. The chapter's moral center is not the altar or the future temple site. It is the interruption: Enough—release your hand. Any theology of power, plague, or punishment that cannot hear that command has mistaken destruction for holiness.
